power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

ethics_statements: The underlying demographic and network data for both TE and AZ were gathered between August and September 2022 as part of the "ENDOW project", and with ethical approval from the London School of Economics and Political Science Research Ethics Committee (Ref. 97257), with residency and other basic information updated immediately prior to the experimental games data collection.

Ethical approval came from the SCI-UM6P ethics review board.
The research design was approved by the London School of Economics and Political Science Research Ethics Committee (ref. 282577).

The underlying demographic data were gathered between April and June 2024 and the network data in December 2024, with ethical approval from the London School of Economics and Political Science Research Ethics Committee (Ref. 326856 and 441059).

The underlying demographic data for UP were gathered between February and June 2024 and the network data in January and February 2025, with ethical approval from the London School of Economics and Political Science Research Ethics Committee (Ref. 326648 and Ref. 480486 respectively).
live_data_statements: Participants were shown 12 recipients per condition in WH and 15 in TZ).
In both communities, participants gave in units of 1000 COP.
Participants gave in amounts of 0, 1/30, 2/30, 3/30, etc.
Participants are first told that they will make Dictator Game allocations in two conditions.

Participants are taught to distinguish the game condition based on a salient visual cue in the Android app (namely, the background colour that appears behind the photograph of the recipient: orange for revealed and blue for anonymous; see Figure 3).

Participants are also informed that none of the allocations are compulsory-i.e., with each allocation decision, they can opt out of making an allocation (cf. Dana et al., 2006; Lazear et al., 2012), with the implications of such a decision explained to them (in such cases, there is no impact on the recipient for whom it effectively has not happened, but for the donor it is treated as an allocation to self of 0).
Participants are asked to allocate an endowment to 14 specific recipients (whose photographs are presented to the participant) per condition.

In NP and UP, participants were asked to make two additional allocations, one per condition, to recipients whose identity they do not know, and whom they are informed will be selected randomly from the adult members of their community.

Participants are initially asked how much they expect they were given by some of the people for whom they appeared as a recipient in Visit 1 (i.e., how much they expect some of their donors gave them).
Participants are then informed of all allocations that were made to them.
Visit 3 concludes with a debrief stage during which participants are paid the total amount they earned from the games and a second show-up fee.
• Payment for accurate expectations -Participants are asked to guess how much five different donors gave them, with close guesses accruing a small additional award.

NP and UP only In addition to the above we also checked: • Condition, enhanced Rather than asking only whether participants could tell the two conditions apart, the participant had to demonstrate that they understood who would, and would not, come to know the identity of the donor in four hypothetical cases • Endowment: whether the participant understood that they had the full endowment available for every allocation, rather than a single endowment to be split across all decisions.

text.text: We conduct experimental economic games designed to study how reputational concern influences people's economic decisions.
Donors make a series of "Dictator Game" decisions, splitting an endowment between themselves and a recipient.
Crucially, recipients are not anonymous strangers, but are other individuals from the same community as the donor, presented to donors via photographs.
By varying the identity of the recipient and whether or not the recipient will come to know the identity of the donor, we can effectively vary the reputational stake of the donor's decision.
We expect that when Dictator Game allocation decisions have greater reputational stakes, donors will be more generous.

Greater reputational stakes could arise from: the revelation of the donor's identity, the social proximity of donor and recipient, and the general network position of donor and recipient, all of which we consider.
We conduct these games in eight rural communities in five countries, where we already have full sociodemographic and social network data on players and their connections.

While there is substantial cross-site variation in the amounts given, we find strikingly similar effects of revelation and social proximity on allocation decisions: in all sites, donors give only slightly more in contexts where their identity is revealed, as opposed to being kept anonymous.
Whether anonymous or revealed, donors give appreciably less to recipients who are more socially distant, with the largest drop occurring between immediate connections and connections-of-connections.
We find mixed evidence that the effect of revealing a donor's identity diminishes with social distance.
Finally, we do not find clear effects for the network position of donor and recipient.
These results improve our understanding of how economic behaviour is intertwined with reputational dynamics in a wide variety of contexts.

While altruistic behaviour does increase with reputational concern cross-culturally, it also appears that in tight-knit, small communities, absence of reputational concern may, contra expectations, lead only to a small increase in selfishness.
How do people act in light of their expectation of others' reactions?
In this paper, we present the results of "lab in the field" experimental economic games wherein participants play not with anonymous partners but with known others from their communities.

Our data are unique in that they they include not only individual-level information, as could be gleaned from standard protocols administered to university students, but also feature complete sociocentric network information describing people's relationships with one another in real-world settings.

By varying whether a donor's decisions are revealed, and the social proximity of donor and recipient, we can vary the reputational stake of decisions, in order to investigate how the scope for reputational concern influences the actions of donors.
Rather than working with ephemeral online samples Deschenaux, I. (2019).
The resilience of caste: Dalits, psychological essentialism, and intercaste marriage in the Himalayan foothills of Eastern Nepal. phd, London School of Economics and Political Science.
or student populations so often studied, we work with adult residents of eight communities in India, Nepal, Colombia, Mexico, and Morocco.

Despite differing markedly in their cultural norms and economic organisation, these communities share one key underlying feature-they are small, enduring, rural communities where residents know one another well, often relying on one another for various types of support.
In such communities, a person's reputation can be of acute importance not only for their relationships, but also for the livelihood and wellbeing.
We invite community members to take part in a series of dictator games, wherein donors are given the opportunity to divide an endowment between themselves and a passive recipient.

While past work has identified that the modal response is generally donors keeping the entire endowment for themselves (as we may expect them to rationally do), many donors typically do give something to the recipient and often split it evenly (see reviews by Engel, 2011; Doñate-Buendía et al., 2022).

text.text: Consequently, the Dictator Game is taken as a measure of generosity or altruism, as well as adherence to norms of fairness or equity (Forsythe et al., 1994; Hoffman et al., 1994; Camerer and Thaler, 1995; Levitt and List, 2007).

text.text: We take advantage of all of these affordances in our experimental design, making the recipients known to the donor and (variably) making the donor known to the recipient.

If recipients learn the identities of donors, and the amount they gave, it opens up their ability to subsequently respond, either through direct reciprocity or by relaying the donor's actions to others (i.e., gossiping), which creates scope for indirect reciprocity as well (Wu et al., 2016).

text.text: These possibilities should in turn trigger concern among donors for how they will be perceived-i.e., image motivation and reputational concern (Bénabou and Tirole, 2006; Andreoni and Bernheim, 2009; Bursztyn and Jensen, 2017)-and strengthen incentives to abide by social norms (Cappelen et al., 2007; López-Pérez, 2008; Krupka and Weber, 2009, 2013; Kimbrough and Vostroknutov, 2016).

text.text: In other words, more generous Dictator Game play may be driven both by a desire to develop a "good" reputation-as someone who behaves "appropriately"-as well as a desire to avoid a "bad" reputation-as someone who behaves "inappropriately".

In line with this, donors have been shown to give more when their identity (conveyed via their name) is revealed to the recipient than when it is kept anonymous, whether they are American undergraduates (Leider et al., 2009), villagers in Paraguay (Ligon and Schechter, 2012, 2020), or residents in a Cairo neighbourhood (Binzel and Fehr, 2013).
text.formatted: In line with this, donors have been shown to give more when their identity (conveyed via their name) is revealed to the recipient than when it is kept anonymous, whether they are American undergraduates <ref type="bibr" target="#b57">(Leider et al., 2009)</ref>, villagers in Paraguay <ref type="bibr">(Ligon and</ref> <ref type="bibr">Schechter, 2012, 2020)</ref>, or residents in a Cairo neighbourhood <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">(Binzel and Fehr, 2013)</ref>.

text.text: Importantly, the effect of the recipient's knowledge of the donor's identity may vary based on features of the donor and recipient: donors may vary in sensitivity to reputational exposure, and exposure to specific recipients may be more reputationally consequential.

First, there is the social proximity of donor and recipient: greater social proximity could make the prospect of future interactions more likely, immediate, and acute, and it could additionally raise the prospect of gossip with common acquaintances, raising the reputational premium of the decision.
In line with this idea, Leider et al. (2009) find that the increase in generosity with "non-anonymity" is greater for socially proximate recipients and for those with more common partners.

text.text: Alternatively, most people have an acute awareness of the reputational standing of their close connections-e.g., with respect to generosity, reciprocity propensity, and general character-which is unlikely to be updated much by a single allocation decision, whereas that same allocation decision might have a much larger marginal effect on standing updating for a more socially distant community member about which the focal has little prior information.
As such, cooperative behaviour directed toward socially distant recipients may carry the greatest reputational premiums.

Second, the overall social position of a known recipient may impact how a donor chooses to behave: a well-connected recipient could share information with many others, who may themselves be wellconnected.

To our knowledge, this has not been directly investigated with the Dictator Game, but related experimental work with third-party observers has shown that people play more cooperatively when they are being monitored by more central observers (e.g., Chandrasekhar et al., 2018; Iacobelli and Singh, 2021).

text.text: Third, the social positions of donors themselves may influence their play.
There are mixed findings for the role of the donor's position on giving rates when play is anonymous (Brañas-Garza et al., 2010; Goeree et al., 2010; Baldassarri and Grossman, 2013).

text.text: The only published work, to our knowledge, exploring how the effect of reveling a donor's identity depends on the social position of the donor is by Ligon and Schechter (2012), who find that (in Paraguayan villages) donors from households with more sharing partners and that spend more on gifts respond to being revealed to give to a chosen person by giving relatively more generously than others.

text.text: Further, the extent to which people are concerned about abiding by such norms may vary from person to person (Kimbrough and Vostroknutov, 2016; Henry and Sonntag, 2019) and by the social positions they occupy (Kovářík et al., 2012).

text.text: Considering the social position of the donor, we can envision two alternatives.
We may first expect that central donors will be particularly concerned with maintaining their good standing within the community, and so be relatively more responsive to revelation.
Alternatively, we may expect that peripheral donors will be relatively more responsive to revelation, given the novel opportunity it provides for them to shape their reputation.
Beyond the dynamics outlined above, the larger sociocultural context could shape donor's allocation decisions.

Different societies (Henrich et al., 2005; Cochard et al., 2021) and even different communities within the same society (Lamba and Mace, 2012) may differ in their norms and institutions, with players' ideas about such norms influencing their own actions (d 'Adda et al., 2020).
text.formatted: Different societies <ref type="bibr" target="#b37">(Henrich et al., 2005;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">Cochard et al., 2021)</ref> and even different communities within the same society <ref type="bibr" target="#b55">(Lamba and Mace, 2012)</ref> may differ in their norms and institutions, with players' ideas about such norms influencing their own actions (d <ref type="bibr">'Adda et al., 2020)</ref>.

text.text: Communities may differ in how they judge apparent transgressions (Barrett et al., 2016), how strictly people are expected to abide by norms (Gelfand et al., 2011; Chua et al., 2019), and the consequences for violating normative expectations (Eriksson et al., 2021).

text.text: Communities may also differ in the extent to which people are interdependent and reliant on one another (Thomson et al., 2018).

text.text: They may differ more generally in their network structure, such as how densely people are connected to one another or how segregated different groups may be from one another.
All of these points of variation may mean that the meaning and implications of generosity will differ, and so too how people behave in such tasks as the Dictator Game (Doñate-Buendía et al., 2022).

text.text: Overall, this body of work demonstrates that the impetus to give in the Dictator Game can vary substantially across scenarios.

Attributes of the donor, the recipient, their relationship to one another, the particular scenario, and the broader context can all induce different motives or incentives that can promote generous play.
Our attention here is particularly on those features which modify what could be termed the social exposure or reputational stake of a person's behaviour.
Assuming that there is no social exposure when an allocation is made anonymously, we focus on the effect of revealing a donor's identity, and variation in the strength of this effect.
Specifically, we ask: Q1 How does revealing a donor's identity to the recipient affect the amount given in a Dictator Game?
Q2 How does the this effect vary with the social proximity of donor and recipient?
Q3 How does this effect vary with the network centrality of donor and recipient?

Our general expectation is that the introduction of a reputational stake will heighten people's motivation to abide by normative expectations-whether personal or social-about how much they should give.
Importantly, different normative expectations could be invoked in the Dictator Game.
One is a general enjoinder to be generous.
A corollary of this would be to not be selfish.
Another is to be fair (Andreoni and Bernheim, 2009; Bicchieri and Chavez, 2010) or to avoid inequity (Fehr and Schmidt, 1999; Bolton and Ockenfels, 2000).
text.formatted: Another is to be fair <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">(Andreoni and Bernheim, 2009;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">Bicchieri and Chavez, 2010)</ref> or to avoid inequity <ref type="bibr">(Fehr and Schmidt, 1999;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">Bolton and Ockenfels, 2000)</ref>.

text.text: These three normative expectations would be reflected by donors: (1) giving more (i.e., being generous), (2) being less likely to give zero (i.e., not being fully selfish), and (3) being more likely to give at least half (i.e., being fair).
text.formatted: These three normative expectations would be reflected by donors: <ref type="bibr">(1)</ref> giving more (i.e., being generous), (2) being less likely to give zero (i.e., not being fully selfish), and (3) being more likely to give at least half (i.e., being fair).

text.text: While ideas of what is fair are, of course, culturally variable (Henrich et al., 2005), existing meta-analyses and theoretical work suggest that giving fifty percent of the total stake is nevertheless salient and worthy of special attention (Engel, 2011; Andreoni and Bernheim, 2009).

text.text: First and foremost, we expect that when their identity is revealed to the recipient (as opposed to being kept anonymous), donors should (H2.1) give more, (H2.2) be more likely to give at least half of their endowment, and (H2.3) be less likely to give exactly zero.

Considering social proximity, we first expect to see a general proximity effect: regardless of condition/revelation, donors should (H1.1) be more generous, (H1.2) be more likely to split the endowment fairly, and (H1.3) be less likely to be selfish towards those whom they are closer to.

We further expect an interaction between revelation and social proximity, but posit two alternative directions: (H3a) the effect of revelation should be stronger among dyads with greater social proximity, as closer recipients can respond more acutely and with greater possible reach.

Alternatively, (H3b) the effect of revelation should be weaker among dyads with greater social proximity, as closer recipients can more readily dismiss and distant recipients more readily learn from the allocation decision.

We next expect an interaction between revelation and the position of the recipient, such that: (H4) the effect of revelation is greater when the recipient is more central as their potential praise, scorn, or sanctioning can have more far-reaching effects.

Finally, we expect an interaction between revelation and the position of the donor, again with two alternatives: (H5a) the effect of revelation should be stronger for more central donors as they have more to lose, or alternatively (H5b) the effect of revelation should be stronger for more peripheral donors as they both have more to gain and will be more sensitive to loosing standing in the eyes of the connections they do have.

Estimated coefficients for M2 suggest that increasing distance could reduce the positive effect of revealing a donor's identity on the probability of giving at least half the endowment.

text.text: We reach no clear conclusions for how allocations are associated with donor centrality, nor for how the effect of social exposure varies with it.
The models present greater compatibility with central donors giving more, but identification is imperfect (pd = 93%).
This is reflected in the positive slope and wide credibility intervals in the middle row of Figure 1.
text.formatted: This is reflected in the positive slope and wide credibility intervals in the middle row of Figure <ref type="figure">1</ref>.

text.text: The models also show greater compatibility with central donors being less likely to give exactly 0 (pd = 91%), but they are fully equivocal on the relationship between donor centrality and giving half or more (pd = 54%).
In addition, they are compatible with either positive and negative changes in the effect of revelation with donor centrality, which leaves us unable to endorse H5a or H5b.
Our within-subject design ensures that each individual donor gives to a wide range of recipients.
This allows for precise identification of any potential relationship between recipient centrality and amount allocated (hence the narrow credibility intervals in the bottom row of Figure 1).
text.formatted: This allows for precise identification of any potential relationship between recipient centrality and amount allocated (hence the narrow credibility intervals in the bottom row of Figure <ref type="figure">1</ref>).

text.text: However, we find no such relation.
As such, we can exclude any large, cross-cultural direct association between recipient centrality and allocation.
Among participants, shifting recipient centrality from the bottom to the top decile is associated with an overall change in allocation of 0.3% [-0.2% to +0.8%] of the total endowment.

Site-wise associations are somewhat more heterogenous, with the notable suggestion of a small but positive association in UP (additional 1.2% [0.4%, 2.1%] of total endowment) and AZ (additional 1.0% [0.03%, 2.1%]).
The change in the effect of revelation when shifting recipient centrality from the bottom to the top decile is -0.35% [-0.97%, 0.24%] of the total endowment.
Expressed relatively, the effect of revelation shrinks to 78% [48%, 120%] its size when changing recipient centrality from bottom to top decile.
Note that H4 is monodirectional: it posits only an increase in the effect of revelation with recipient centrality.
The model is compatible, at most, with a fairly small effect in this direction.
Thus, we conclude that H4 is either wrong-there could be a sizeable negative interaction between revelation and recipient centrality-or, at best, correct but arguably negligible in size.

To ensure that montonicity constraints imposed by our models do not dissimulate a U-shaped relation between donor or alter centrality on the one hand, and allocations or the effect of revelation on the other, we additionally fit models without these constraints.
We find no sign of such a relation.
See SI D.
It is worth noting that these results describe how allocations and the effect of revelation vary with centrality while keeping other donor and recipient characteristics constant.
In reality, individuals cannot easily change their centrality, and centrality is correlated with other measures that enter the model.
Computing average fitted values by observed centrality reveals that donors in the top and third (but not second) decile are predicted to give substantially more than others, on average.
This must be because of their distinct covariate profile and individual characteristics captured by random intercepts.
No analogous finding holds for recipient centrality, nor for the interaction of revelation and donor or recipient centrality.
SI E offers more detail.

Examining the random effects in the models, we find substantial unexplained heterogeneity at the donor and donor-household level, both in terms of the average amount given and responsiveness to condition.
This suggests that some participants-and, to a degree, participants from the same household-are consistently more or less generous than others.
Similarly, there is systematic variation in how they respond to social exposure.
In contrast, unexplained heterogeneity at the recipient level is low: specific individuals do not appear to systematically attract smaller or larger allocations from different donors.
See SI F for further details.
These strong donor effects may be down to individual personality, but it is also possible that parts of this variation could be explained by unmeasured characteristics.
We fit a second set of models adding terms for donor and recipient age, gender, and household wealth.

Estimated model coefficients for centrality and distance are remarkably similar in these models, suggesting that the associations reported above are not confounded by these demographic measures (see SI B and Figures S7, S8, S9).

text.text: For exploratory purposes, we consider the coefficient estimates for these demographic predictors in M1 (see Figure S10).
text.formatted: For exploratory purposes, we consider the coefficient estimates for these demographic predictors in M1 (see Figure <ref type="figure">S10</ref>).

text.text: These suggest that in most communities, men give more than women.
Other demographic effects display more cultural variation.
For example, older donors give less in all South Asian sites (TE, AZ, NP, UP), and older recipients are given more in TM (Mexcico), WL (Colombia), NP (Nepal), and UP (India).
Notably, we find no evidence that the wealth of donor and recipient influence allocations, despite participants regularly reporting that they allocated according to need.
We also find no cross-cultural interaction between these demographic predictors and the effect of revelation.
There is however a suggestion that older donors may be less sensitive to revelation in TE (India) and WL (Colombia).

The communities in which we conducted these Dictator Games differ markedly from the anonymous online or student populations in which economic games are so often administered-most notably by being rural, dense in kin, highly dependent on mutual aid and support provisioning, and featuring enduring social relationships spanning decades, if not generations.
It is precisely in such contexts that we believe reputational cognition is best studied.

In these communities, residents are often intimately involved in one another's lives, and are used to either making or declining to make support provisioning ties that carry real-world consequences for how they are perceived by others (e.g., as generous, selfish, or prestigious).
We presume (and indeed show in Redhead et al., 2024 Redhead et al., , 2026) ) that reputational considerations then guide future economic decisions.
text.formatted: We presume (and indeed show in <ref type="bibr" target="#b74">Redhead et al., 2024</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b75">Redhead et al., , 2026) )</ref> that reputational considerations then guide future economic decisions.

text.text: Although we do not have a comprehensive sample of human cultural diversity, these eight rural communities in India, Nepal, Mexico, Morocco, and Colombia differ markedly in terms of social organisation, local norms and beliefs, modes of subsistence, levels of market integration, religion, and a host of other variables.

The recently settled Amazigh nomadic herders of the TZ community in the High Atlas mountains of Morocco live very different lives than the Tzotzil Mayan smallholder farmers of the TM community in Chiapas, Mexico, or the farmers and wage labourers of the UP community in Uttar Pradesh, India.
In light of this diversity, it is no surprise that the allocation distributions vary so strongly across communities.

Our results therefore confirm the cultural variation noted in prior work (Henrich et al., 2005; Doñate-Buendía et al., 2022): local norms, presumably stabilised over extended periods, appear to govern how much individuals typically share in the Dictator Game, despite the Dictator Game itself being novel to most participants.
text.formatted: Our results therefore confirm the cultural variation noted in prior work <ref type="bibr" target="#b37">(Henrich et al., 2005;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Doñate-Buendía et al., 2022)</ref>: local norms, presumably stabilised over extended periods, appear to govern how much individuals typically share in the Dictator Game, despite the Dictator Game itself being novel to most participants.

text.text: This does not mean, however, that there are no cross-cultural regularities.
We find a small but consistent effect of revealing the donor's identity to the recipient.
Across the varied settings, donors are responsive to the reputational stake of their decisions.
Revealing their identity to the recipient causes them to give more, and makes them more likely to give half or more of their endowment, and less likely to give exactly zero.

The effects we find in the different communities are consistent in sign and magnitude, which suggests that the reputational motivations at play might transcend culturally varying normative expectations.

Our results suggest that the well-established association between social proximity and generosity holds cross-culturally: in all communities, donors are more generous with others with whom they are more closely connected.
Our design allows us to comment on the mechanism that underlies greater generosity towards socially proximate others.

Were this association driven only by the increased reputational concern one feels in one's immediate social circle, we would only find an association between social distance and amount allocated when the donor's identity is revealed to the recipient.
In fact, the association holds even when the donor's identity is kept anonymous.
We find mixed evidence suggesting that it is weaker in this case, but we establish firmly that it is still present.

This is in line with prior findings on social distance with anonymous donors (Leider et al., 2009; Brañas-Garza et al., 2010; Goeree et al., 2010; Ligon and Schechter, 2012; Binzel and Fehr, 2013; Candelo et al., 2018; Robson, 2021), but here we are better able to disentangle the possible mechanisms at play.
text.formatted: This is in line with prior findings on social distance with anonymous donors <ref type="bibr" target="#b57">(Leider et al., 2009;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">Brañas-Garza et al., 2010;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b34">Goeree et al., 2010;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b59">Ligon and Schechter, 2012;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">Binzel and Fehr, 2013;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">Candelo et al., 2018;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b79">Robson, 2021)</ref>, but here we are better able to disentangle the possible mechanisms at play.

text.text: Even when they remain anonymous, donors may be driven by in-group favouritism (Balliet et al., 2014) or "social discounting" (Jones and Rachlin, 2006), and they may have greater "stake" in proximate partners due to greater interdependence (Roberts, 2005; Aktipis et al., 2018) and even biological relatedness (cf. Macfarlan and Quinlan, 2008; Gervais, 2017; Pisor et al., 2020; Ross and Pisor, 2025).
text.formatted: Even when they remain anonymous, donors may be driven by in-group favouritism <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">(Balliet et al., 2014)</ref> or "social discounting" <ref type="bibr" target="#b45">(Jones and Rachlin, 2006)</ref>, and they may have greater "stake" in proximate partners due to greater interdependence <ref type="bibr" target="#b78">(Roberts, 2005;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">Aktipis et al., 2018)</ref> and even biological relatedness (cf. <ref type="bibr" target="#b62">Macfarlan and Quinlan, 2008;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b31">Gervais, 2017;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b67">Pisor et al., 2020;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b82">Ross and Pisor, 2025)</ref>.

text.text: Thus, while increased reputational concern may partly explain generosity towards proximate others, other mechanisms must also be at play.

In our initial hypotheses on the interplay of reputation and social distance, we formulated some opposite-direction predictions: participants could be reputationally "conservative"-i.e., primarily concerned with maintaining reputation in their immediate entourage-or they could be reputationally "eager"-primarily seeking to gain reputation in the eyes of distant others.

Our results lend greater credence to the former than the latter, albeit equivocally: for one of the three outcomes, the effect of revealing a donor's identity is stronger when the recipient is socially proximate.
For the other two, results are less clear but nevertheless show greater compatibility with this possibility than with the opposite.
To our surprise, we find no systematic pattern when considering the donor and recipient's positions in their community.
While the middle row in Figure 1 suggests a positive association between donor centrality and amount allocated, credibility intervals are wide.
text.formatted: While the middle row in Figure <ref type="figure">1</ref> suggests a positive association between donor centrality and amount allocated, credibility intervals are wide.

text.text: We are left uncertain as to whether the social prominence of donors is associated with greater or lesser generosity, and we are completely uncertain about whether they show greater or lesser sensitivity to reputational exposure.

With regards to recipients, we can exclude the possibility that there is any non-negligible, cross-site, systematic association between a recipient's centrality and the amount they are given (contra work on the centrality of third party monitors: e.g., Chandrasekhar et al., 2018; Breza and Chandrasekhar, 2019; Iacobelli and Singh, 2021).
text.formatted: With regards to recipients, we can exclude the possibility that there is any non-negligible, cross-site, systematic association between a recipient's centrality and the amount they are given (contra work on the centrality of third party monitors: e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">Chandrasekhar et al., 2018;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">Breza and Chandrasekhar, 2019;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b44">Iacobelli and Singh, 2021)</ref>.

text.text: If donors are in fact more or less generous towards socially prominent recipients, our findings suggest that it is to a degree so small that it arguably does not matter in practice.

Moreover, the effect of social exposure either diminishes substantially when giving to more prominent recipients, or increases so little that we can consider it effectively unchanged (contra Ligon and Schechter, 2012).
text.formatted: Moreover, the effect of social exposure either diminishes substantially when giving to more prominent recipients, or increases so little that we can consider it effectively unchanged (contra <ref type="bibr" target="#b59">Ligon and Schechter, 2012)</ref>.

text.text: Taken at face value, this result suggests that one of the fundamental assumptions we made when designing the study was mistaken: we had speculated that because central individuals exercise more control over the flow of information in their communities, people would behave more generously towards them in the revealed condition.
This does not appear to be the case.
Overall, the average effect of revelation we observe is relatively small .
A number of reasons could explain this modest effect size.
One is the relative lack of salience and immediacy of revelation in our design, as this happens several days after the allocation and without the donor being physically present.

Studies where revelation is immediate and visible to all (e.g., Frey and Bohnet, 1995; Bohnet and Frey, 1999) typically find stronger effects than those where revelation is indirect (e.g., Rotella et al., 2021).
text.formatted: Studies where revelation is immediate and visible to all (e.g., <ref type="bibr">Frey and Bohnet, 1995;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">Bohnet and Frey, 1999)</ref> typically find stronger effects than those where revelation is indirect (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b85">Rotella et al., 2021)</ref>.

text.text: Alternatively, it may be that the "anonymous" condition did not feel truly anonymous to participants, for example, because of the presence of the interviewer recording allocations on a tablet.
The extent to which decisions are transparent to experimenters is known to influence play (Hoffman et al., 1994 (Hoffman et al., , 1996;; Lamba and Mace, 2010).
text.formatted: The extent to which decisions are transparent to experimenters is known to influence play <ref type="bibr" target="#b41">(Hoffman et al., 1994</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b42">(Hoffman et al., , 1996;;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b54">Lamba and Mace, 2010)</ref>.

text.text: Moreover, in small, face-to-face societies where gossip is common, people may not believe secrecy is a viable option; they may be disposed towards believing that their actions will, eventually, be revealed publicly regardless or our assurances to the contrary.
We even speculate that the small effect size may reflect an important sensitivity to reputational bookkeeping.

In our framing, we follow past work (e.g., Ligon and Schechter, 2012) in implicitly assuming that motives for giving in the anonymous condition (for a self-interested agent) are small, and they would only become large in the revealed condition if agents were behaving so as to minimize the social sanctioning that might follow from giving less than what is viewed as appropriate by a recipient.
text.formatted: In our framing, we follow past work (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b59">Ligon and Schechter, 2012)</ref> in implicitly assuming that motives for giving in the anonymous condition (for a self-interested agent) are small, and they would only become large in the revealed condition if agents were behaving so as to minimize the social sanctioning that might follow from giving less than what is viewed as appropriate by a recipient.

text.text: However, it is possible that this framing is wrong-rational, reputationally risk-sensitive agents might prefer to behave similarly in both anonymous and revealed conditions either because they are following internal norms to behave in public like they would in private (doing the right thing either way), or strategically bet-hedging against reputational loss that would come from 'anonymous' behaviour that comes to light.
We also know that some participants did not fully comprehend the difference between conditions.
Dropping those who failed comprehension checks, however, does not affect results (see Figures S32 and S33), which offers some reassurance against this threat.
text.formatted: Dropping those who failed comprehension checks, however, does not affect results (see Figures <ref type="figure" target="#fig_1">S32</ref> and <ref type="figure" target="#fig_1">S33</ref>), which offers some reassurance against this threat.

text.text: Finally, and most interestingly, it may simply be that, in these relatively small, close-knit communities, donors are relatively unconcerned with how public their decisions are, letting other considerations be front of mind when making allocations.
Reputational concern is obviously not the only factor that encourages generosity, and it may be secondary to other considerations in these settings.
This study establishes many avenues for future work.
At the measurement level, there is a need to validate results obtained with the photograph-driven, asynchronous protocol we used.
It is likely that this design attenuates effects when compared to a synchronous design in which donor and recipient are physically present at the time of allocation, but we do not know how strongly.

On a substantive level, further studies are needed to consolidate our emergent understanding of how reputational concern and social distance interact, and we need more work to check whether the absence of an effect for recipient centrality is robust.

Finally, additional modelling work on the data we have collected may yield new insights: in particular, models allowing for latent classes among donors may help us better understand the behavioural heterogeneity that our data suggests exists even within each community.
Much theoretical and empirical work has sought to establish how reputation and reputational concern shapes people's behaviour and relationships (Giardini and Wittek, 2019).
text.formatted: Much theoretical and empirical work has sought to establish how reputation and reputational concern shapes people's behaviour and relationships <ref type="bibr" target="#b33">(Giardini and Wittek, 2019)</ref>.

text.text: Yet, there are still many outstanding questions on how this transpires in practice (Giardini et al., 2022).
text.formatted: Yet, there are still many outstanding questions on how this transpires in practice <ref type="bibr" target="#b32">(Giardini et al., 2022)</ref>.

text.text: We offer this design and these findings as a potential avenue for further exploration, coupling some degree of experimental control with the complex and multifaceted motivations that form the substance of people's actual day-to-day interactions and decisions.
We conduct Dictator Games with adult residents in eight communities in five countries.
Our key design choice is that players are paired with other residents in the same community, presented to them via photographs.

We implement the games using a newly-developed Android app for behavioural economic and peer-report data, based on software (Ross and Redhead, 2022) designed to facilitate running the network-structured behavioural economic games (Gervais, 2017).
text.formatted: We implement the games using a newly-developed Android app for behavioural economic and peer-report data, based on software <ref type="bibr" target="#b83">(Ross and Redhead, 2022)</ref> designed to facilitate running the network-structured behavioural economic games <ref type="bibr" target="#b31">(Gervais, 2017)</ref>.

text.text: Participants could opt to give an amount of their choice, in 10% increments of the total endowment (0%, 10%, . . . , 100%.
Other increments were used in some sites, see SI G).

Each participant makes decisions in two conditions: in the "anonymous" condition, recipients will be informed of the amount allocated to them, but not who made the allocation; in the "revealed" (a) Anonymous (b) Revealed condition, recipients will be informed of the amount allocated to them and shown the photograph of the person who made the allocation (they will also be asked to rate the appropriateness of the amount given).
Donors know in which condition they are making each decision.
That is, donors know whether their identity will be revealed to the recipient to whom they are (possibly) allocating money.

By using social network information for each community to build a list of dyadic pairings, we are able to ensure that there is variation in the relative position and social proximity of recipients for each donor.

In short, the different pairings of donor and recipient (across the two conditions) should entail variation in the extent to which there is a reputational stake for the donor, and so consequent variation in how they play.
The full protocol entailed three visits to each participant, spread over a number of days (see SI H for more details).
Each participant was shown 14 recipients in one condition, then 14 in the other (see Figure 3 for a demonstration of how this appears to participants in the app.
text.formatted: Each participant was shown 14 recipients in one condition, then 14 in the other (see Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_1">3</ref> for a demonstration of how this appears to participants in the app.

text.text: Participants were shown 12 recipients per condition in WH and 15 in TZ).
Condition order was randomised across participants.
Recipients were drawn from across the community, with deliberate oversampling of high-and low-centrality recipients, to ensure that each participant makes allocations to a broad range of others.
The allocations were economically motivated decisions: participants knew that some of their decisions would be selected to be paid out.

The endowment for each allocation decision was determined with consideration of local daily wage labour rates and monetary denominations, and a general aim for comparability across sites. 1We ran the same general design, with some modifications, in eight communities: "TE" and "AZ" in Tamil Nadu, India; "WH" and "WL" in western Colombia; "TZ" in the High Atlas Mountains of Morocco; "TM" in Chiapas, Mexico; "NP" in eastern Nepal, and "UP" in Uttar Pradesh, India.

text.text: In each community, we have comprehensive sociodemographic data that allows us to characterise participants in terms of their age, gender, material wealth, etc.
Table S6 reports the demographics of donors across the communities.
text.formatted: Table <ref type="table">S6</ref> reports the demographics of donors across the communities.

text.text: We further have extensive information on the social connections linking residents together.
This includes self-reported social support relationships, covering a range of different types of support, both material and immaterial.
SI I describes the network data in more detail.
Here, we use an aggregate network constructed from the combination of the various relationship types to construct a single network representing the flows of support between residents.
Plots of the networks are shown in Figure S24.
text.formatted: Plots of the networks are shown in Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_0">S24</ref>.

text.text: Table S7 reports the number of observations for the different elements of the experimental design in each community.
text.formatted: Table <ref type="table">S7</ref> reports the number of observations for the different elements of the experimental design in each community.

text.text: Our coverage is quite high, with an overall participation rate of 77% of all adult residents across communities.
Non-participation was primarily due to people being unreachable at the time of data collection.
SI G presents basic details on each community and describes site-specific deviations from the general design.
Two site-specific deviations warrant noting here.
First, in WH and TZ, participants saw the same recipients across both conditions, as opposed to different recipients.
Second, in TZ norms of propriety meant that we could not use photographs, but instead gave the names of the recipients along with their birth year and the names of their parents.
A central focus in our analyses is on the position and proximity of players.

To characterise the position of players, we use PageRank centrality, which broadly identifies nodes in a network that are structurally important, in that other structurally important nodes connect to them.
Details on the transformations we apply to make centrality measures commensurable across communities are offered in the next section.

For the social proximity of donor i and recipient j, we use the shortest path between themi.e., how many intermediaries it would take to connect i and j, when being maximally efficient in traversing the network.
If two people are friends, they will have a distance of one, if they are friends-of-friends, they will have a distance of two, etc.
Summaries of these measures are presented in Table 2.
text.formatted: Summaries of these measures are presented in Table <ref type="table">2</ref>.

text.text: We use ordered beta regression (Kubinec, 2023) for model M1 (where the raw allocations are the outcome), using the ordbetareg package in R, which builds on brms (Bürkner, 2018).
text.formatted: We use ordered beta regression <ref type="bibr" target="#b52">(Kubinec, 2023)</ref> for model M1 (where the raw allocations are the outcome), using the ordbetareg package in R, which builds on brms <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">(Bürkner, 2018)</ref>.

text.text: Ordered beta regression is designed specifically for zero-and one-inflated proportions, and is therefore well-suited to modelling the share of a total endowment given in a Dictator Game.
We fit logistic regression models for the other two-derived-binary outcomes.

We use the same set of predictors and the same random effect structure across models, with one exception: the "precision" parameter (ϕ), which governs dispersion in the ordered beta model and does not exist in logistic regression, is modelled as a site-wise random intercept.
The R code specifying the model form is available in SI J.
The predictors and random effect structure are described in Table S9.
text.formatted: The predictors and random effect structure are described in Table <ref type="table">S9</ref>.

text.text: The hierarchical structure maps onto the nesting of our data: allocations are nested within site, donor (each participant makes multiple allocations), recipient (the same recipient appears as a partner for different donors), donor-recipient dyad (when dyads were repeated across conditions), donor and recipient household (this also accounts for the fact that our measure of wealth is at household level), and research assistants.
We include random intercepts for all these levels.

In selecting random slopes, we loosely follow the injunction to "keep it maximal" (Barr et al., 2013), ensuring in particular that we include donor-and site-level random slopes for the fixed effects against which we test hypotheses.
text.formatted: In selecting random slopes, we loosely follow the injunction to "keep it maximal" <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">(Barr et al., 2013)</ref>, ensuring in particular that we include donor-and site-level random slopes for the fixed effects against which we test hypotheses.

text.text: We omit random slopes where we have insufficient data to identify them (for example, at household and dyad levels) and where their inclusion creates unnecessary computational burden (Matuschek et al., 2017).
text.formatted: We omit random slopes where we have insufficient data to identify them (for example, at household and dyad levels) and where their inclusion creates unnecessary computational burden <ref type="bibr" target="#b63">(Matuschek et al., 2017)</ref>.

text.text: In particular, we do not include random slopes at the recipient level, as early attempts suggested little to no heterogeneity at this level.
We treat network centrality and social distance as ordered categorical rather than numeric variables (see Table S10).
text.formatted: We treat network centrality and social distance as ordered categorical rather than numeric variables (see Table <ref type="table">S10</ref>).

text.text: This allows us to model their effects as monotonic but non-linear (Bürkner and Charpentier, 2018).
text.formatted: This allows us to model their effects as monotonic but non-linear <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">(Bürkner and Charpentier, 2018)</ref>.

text.text: The rationale for doing this rests on the observation that incremental increases in centrality mean very different things at different parts of the centrality distribution.
Generally, influence or prominence is not evenly distributed, but rather concentrated among a restricted number of individuals at the top of the centrality distribution.
Similarly, incremental steps are qualitatively different at low and high distances.
We use weakly regularising priors form most parameters, and improper flat priors for populationlevel fixed effects.
Model diagnostics are included in SI K and prior sensitivity checks in SI L.
Incomplete coverage of the underlying network data would force us to drop almost a quarter of the observations.
To prevent this, we imputed values by simulating new networks from the observed ones.

We fit an exponential random graph model to the full network of adult residents and simulate outgoing edges for residents who did not provide responses for the social support survey (Krause et al., 2020).
text.formatted: We fit an exponential random graph model to the full network of adult residents and simulate outgoing edges for residents who did not provide responses for the social support survey <ref type="bibr" target="#b48">(Krause et al., 2020)</ref>.

text.text: We then calculate measures of centrality and social proximity from these imputed networks.

Imputing with an exponential random graph model (ERGM) is superior to standard multiple imputation done directly on the dataset, because such techniques would treat each allocation pairing as independent, while the ERGM can account for higher-order associations between dyads (e.g., the effect of having friends in common on the prospect of a tie).
Further details are included in SI I.3.
For a small number of observations where demographic correlates were missing, we additionally conducted multiple imputation using the R package mice.
We fit models to 25 imputed datasets, comfortably in excess of recommended figures for this amount of missing data (van Buuren, 2018).
text.formatted: We fit models to 25 imputed datasets, comfortably in excess of recommended figures for this amount of missing data <ref type="bibr" target="#b89">(van Buuren, 2018)</ref>.

text.text: Because of the computational costs of fitting complex models in a Bayesian workflow, we only do this for two main model specifications per outcome.
We then combine the posterior draws from all 25 models into a single object (Zhou and Reiter, 2010).
text.formatted: We then combine the posterior draws from all 25 models into a single object <ref type="bibr" target="#b92">(Zhou and Reiter, 2010)</ref>.

text.text: Coefficients and credible intervals for the resulting models are extremely similar to those fit when dropping partial cases (see SI K), but using imputed models allows us to include participants we would otherwise drop in the calculation of predicted values and marginal effects.
In the results section above, we report effect sizes on the outcome scale.
These are obtained following principles outlined in Arel-Bundock (2025).

All estimates are computed using "counterfactual grids": they represent the mean predicted effect of changing values for one variable, in our observed data, while keeping other covariates at their observed levels.
We use weights to compensate for the unequal size of the different sites, and our deliberate over-sampling of central recipients.

We did not attempt this.

We do not address it.

text.text: Note that the coefficients for the top facet are on a different scale to the bottom two facets, because of cut-off points in ordered beta regression.
When comparing across models, compare only the sign, not the scale.
The "Revealed" predictor corresponds to the effect of revealing the allocation to the recipient.
"Distance" is the geodesic distance between donor and recipient in the social network; the coefficient here is for the average effect of increasing distance by 1.
"Donor centrality" and "Recipient centrality" correspond to the Pagerank centrality of donor and recipient; coefficients represent the average effect of moving up one one decile in centrality.

To assess how partial pooling affects coefficient estimates in model M1, we fit eight additional models using the same specification but restricting the data to each community.
The coefficient estimates from these models are therefore estimated without any pooling.
The results are shown in Figures S11.
As it is designed to, partial pooling pulls site-level estimates towards the overall population-level parameter.

This has a noticeable effect on estimates of the effect of revelation (and its interaction with other parameters), in particular for sites where the no-pooling estimates have wide posterior Credibility Intervals.
Unlike their partialpooling counterparts, no-pooling estimates for revelation are compatible with a zero-or negative effect-sizes for several communities: WH, TM, TE, AZ.
In the main text of the article, we claim that the effect of revelation is cross-culturally consistent.
No-pooling estimates are still compatible with this claim-the credibility interval for all no-pooling estimates encompasses the overall estimated fixed effect-but some caution may be warranted.

Nevertheless, there is no reason to believe that no-pooling estimates are superior, and we note that where there is clear cross-cultural heterogeneity-as is the case for the Intercept-partial-pooling models clearly recovers it.
H5a and H5b (see Table S1) suggest that peripheral, respectively central, donors will react more strongly to the effect of revelation.

text.text: One possibility that we do not contemplate in the main text is that the both of these claims are true, i.e., that the relationship between donor centrality and the effect of revelation is U-shaped.
The models we use in the artilce include a monotonicity constraint for the effect of donorcentrality; which means they cannot recover this kind of relation, even if the data suggest it exists.
To assuage this concern, we additionally fit a model in which donor and alter centrality deciles are modelled as a simple categorical variable, using complete-case only for computational efficiency.
Figure S12 shows resulting model predictions.
text.formatted: Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_5">S12</ref> shows resulting model predictions.

text.text: We find no evidence of a U-shaped relationship between donor centrality and the effect of revelation.
For completeness, we show the relation between donor centrality and allocations (rather than the effect of revelation) in Figure S13.

text.text: The estimated effect sizes and model predictions reported in the main text and used to generate figures were obtained following principles laid out in Arel-Bundock (2025).
Three aspects of our workflow are worth describing in detail, because they influence how the resulting effect sizes and associated credibility intervals should be interpreted.
Prediction grid.
We use an "empirical grid" to generate model predictions, creating counterfactual values for the variables whose effect size we wish to estimate.
For instance, when computing how the effect of revelation changes with distance, we start with a grid containing our actual observations.
We replicate this entire grid multiple times, fixing the values of distance and condition to all their possible combinations but keeping other covariates at their observed values.
We then generate predicted values for all the resulting combinations, using a large number of posterior draws, and use these to compute and summarise predictions and contrasts of interest.
A limitation of this procedure is that the counterfactual grids we use can contain unrealistic observations.
For example, the procedure allows us to ask how fixing donors' centrality to the bottom vs top decile affects the outcome, on average, while keeping other donor characteristics constant.

This counterfactual estimation of the effect of donor centrality is correct from a modelling standpoint and adequately translates model parameters into interpretable effect sizes on the outcome scale, but in reality an individual's network centrality is not something that can change easily, and it is correlated with other covariates (e.g., gender, age, etc.).
It is also possible to compute effect sizes summarised by observed levels of a variable of interest.
The trade-off is that effect sizes computed in this way are no longer "conditional" on keeping other variables constant-but they do avoid implausible counterfactuals.
For an illustation, see Fig S16, which shows the effect of revelation by donor centrality computed using the two different approaches.
text.formatted: For an illustation, see Fig <ref type="figure">S16</ref>, which shows the effect of revelation by donor centrality computed using the two different approaches.

text.text: While summarising effects by observed values is informative, we do not use it in the main text because we believe it is further removed from how readers will typically interpret effect sizes.
Random effects.
When computing predicted model values, we include all random effects estimated in the model (i.e. we include site-, donor-, recipient-, household-, and dyad-level effects).

As a result, the estimated effect sizes and credibility intervals are specific to the sample which we observed, not necessarily valid for any theoretical superpopulation from which our observations are drawn-they are analogous, in this sense, to a "Sample Average Treatment Effect" (SATE, but see the remarks below on weighting).
Importantly, when testing hypotheses in the main text, we refer to estimated fixed-effect parameters, not computed effect sizes.

Conditional on our model being correct, the fixed effect paramaters and associated credibility intervals are valid for a theoeretical superpopulation of sites, participants, etc. from which our observed sites, participants, etc. would be randomly sampled.
Weighting.
When computing average predictions and effect sizes for a given site, we give each donor and recipient equal weight.
When computing average predictions and effect sizes across sites, we additionally give each site equal weight.
This post-stratification strategy compensates both for our deliberate over-sampling of peripeheral and central recipients, and the the different sample sizes in each site.
If we did not weight each site equally, our estimates would be severely over-influenced by South Asia, where the four communities with the highest number of observations as situated.
The trade-off is that our strategy gives vastly more weight to individuals in small sites.
At the extreme, observations from WH (Colombia) will carry, on average, 14.5 times more weight than those from UP (India).

In practice, the problem is not as severe as it may seem, because the use of partial pooling in our model will move estimated coefficients for small sites, such as WH, more than for large sites such as UP.
Consider the effect of revelation: using equal sites for each site, we report in the main text that donors give 1.5% [1.2%, 1.7%] more of the initial endowment on average, acrross sites.
If we do not use equal weighting for each site, the figure becomes 1.6% [1.4%, 1.8%].

We aimed to make the data across communities as comparable as possible, but there are points of divergence in the underlying data and data collection protocols, which are outlined below, along with additional background information on each community.
The TE and AZ communities are two neighbouring villages (separated by a few kilometres) located in Sivagangai District, Tamil Nadu, India.
Residents engage in a mix of agriculture (mostly rice, sugar cane, cotton, banana, and coconut) and wage labour in nearby towns and cities.
The nearest market towns are about ten minutes drive away, and the nearest city of Madurai (with a few million inhabitants) is roughly a one hour drive away.
Residents are members of a mix of caste and religious groups (Hindus, Catholics, and Protestants), with these divisions structuring much of people's interactions with one another.
In TE, Dalit (also often referred to as Scheduled Caste) groups make up the numerical majority in this village, holding many positions of leadership, and many households are relatively well off.

In AZ, the balance of particular caste and religious groups is slightly different, with a smaller number of Dalit (or Scheduled Caste) residents who are consequently somewhat more relegated and disadvantaged compared to others.
People are certainly concerned with maintaining a "good name" in their community and avoiding negative gossip and enviousness.
Eleanor Power has been conducting fieldwork in the community since 2011 (see, e.g., Power, 2017; Power and Ready, 2018; Power, 2018; Power and Ready, 2019).

The TZ site is located in the Ait Hani district in the High Atlas of Morocco, about an hour and a half drive from the town of Tinghir (pop ∼ 45, 000).
The community is a small village (approximately 450 residents), comprised mostly of families which were formerly nomadic herders, now largely settling down.
Livelihoods combine wage labour with subsistence agriculture and animal husbandry.
Crops include apples, alfalfa, barley, and wheat, with women performing most of the agricultural labour.
Most men engage in wage labour, particularly in construction, while a smaller proportion work as shopkeepers, government employees, or entrepreneurs.

Lineage is an important marker of identity and solidarity in the village, and cooperation is regulated through shared institutions, including rotational irrigation overseen by a water custodian (Anghar n Aman), male-led community associations, and a tribal elder (Sheikh Al-Qbila) who mediates with the state.
Wealth differs sharply between households, and villagers describe a close community in which gossip, social comparison, and obligations are part of daily life.

text.text: TM is largely monolingual Tzotzil; aside from the school teachers who work at the local state primary school, few of its residents speak Spanish.

Most of TM's residents practice Maya (a) Anonymous (b) Revealed Traditionally, these farmers have practiced milpa agriculture, a lowintensity polyculture system in which farmers grow multiple crops at once, mainly the native varieties of yellow maize and black beans of the region.
During the past 15 years, local farmers have sought to diversify their production, increasingly clearing land to grow cash crops such as coffee, avocados, and a variety of other fruit trees.
Nevertheless, milpa agriculture remains nearly universal and families continue to rely on yellow corn and black beans for subsistence.
As in most indigenous communities in Chiapas, TM is governed autonomously.

The community has its own system of offices, or "cargo system," by which compulsory civil or religious offices are rotated between households periodically-as has been typical among the Mayan communities of Chiapas for decades Cancian (1965).

text.text: The community nominates its officeholders through communal assemblies which heads of household (usually male) are mandated to attend.
Individuals who refuse to accept a nomination are sanctioned with a hefty fee.
The cargo system's offices can be heavily burdensome and time consuming, requiring incumbents to serve the community for two years or spending up to three times an annual income in rituals.
Successful service in these offices tends to be rewarded with recognition from the community and a reputational boost to the officeholder.

text.text: The Android application works in conjunction with an R package that builds the game settings and pairings.
This allows us to build code templates in R, creating donor-recipient pairs on the basis of whatever covariate data we choose to supply.
We can then conduct the games asynchronously, showing photographs of multiple recipients to donors sequentially, and paying out these allocations at a later stage.
Decisions are motivated: real money is at stake.
However, we do not pay respondents for every decision they make, or for every decision made towards them.

We randomly select four decisions to be paid out: two decisions are ones where the respondent was a donor to people in the community (they get paid what they chose to keep for themselves), and two decisions are ones where the respondent received money from others (they get paid the amount that the others gave them).

The choice to pay two decision "halves" rather than one "full" decision was made to ensure equitable payment, as the oversampling of some players would otherwise lead to greater payout opportunities for some.
We now outline the general data collection procedure.
Notable variations to this design at any site are noted briefly in the description of each site above.
The study requires three visits to each participant (see Figure S21 for a schematic).

text.text: During the preliminary visit (Visit 1), we acquire consent for the study and take a photograph of the participant, explaining how this will be used.
Everyone who gives consent is included in the games.
In Visit 2, participants again give consent, are introduced to the game rules, and complete a comprehension check.
They then make allocations in Dictator Games under two conditionsone in which their identity is kept anonymous and the other in which it is revealed to the recipient.
Participants are first told that they will make Dictator Game allocations in two conditions.
In all communities except for NP (Nepal) and UP (India), they receive explanations for both conditions at the outset, then make allocations in both conditions.
In NP and UP, they receive explanations for the first condition, complete corresponding allocations, then received explanations for the second condition and complete corresponding allocations.

Participants are taught to distinguish the game condition based on a salient visual cue in the Android app (namely, the background colour that appears behind the photograph of the recipient: orange for revealed and blue for anonymous; see Figure 3).
text.formatted: Participants are taught to distinguish the game condition based on a salient visual cue in the Android app (namely, the background colour that appears behind the photograph of the recipient: orange for revealed and blue for anonymous; see Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_1">3</ref>).

text.text: Participants are also informed that none of the allocations are compulsory-i.e., with each allocation decision, they can opt out of making an allocation (cf. Dana et al., 2006; Lazear et al., 2012), with the implications of such a decision explained to them (in such cases, there is no impact on the recipient for whom it effectively has not happened, but for the donor it is treated as an allocation to self of 0).
text.formatted: Participants are also informed that none of the allocations are compulsory-i.e., with each allocation decision, they can opt out of making an allocation (cf. <ref type="bibr" target="#b30">Dana et al., 2006;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b56">Lazear et al., 2012)</ref>, with the implications of such a decision explained to them (in such cases, there is no impact on the recipient for whom it effectively has not happened, but for the donor it is treated as an allocation to self of 0).

text.text: Conditions are presented sequentially and the order in which they are presented is randomised.
This is done in order to control for ordering effects.
Participants are asked to allocate an endowment to 14 specific recipients (whose photographs are presented to the participant) per condition.

In NP and UP, participants were asked to make two additional allocations, one per condition, to recipients whose identity they do not know, and whom they are informed will be selected randomly from the adult members of their community.
This appears as the eighth allocation in each condition.

After participants make allocations, RAs provide a second, overall assessment of comprehension following game play to act as a confirmatory checkpoint, or as an opportunity to revise the previous assessment of comprehension.
Participants then make a first round of reputational evaluations for several key others in the community-e.g., How generous do you think this person is?
How fair do you think this person is?
(see Figure S22).
text.formatted: (see Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_10">S22</ref>).

text.text: Visit 2 concludes with the payout of a participation/show-up fee.

In Visit 3, we ask participants how much they expect to have received from various donors, inform participants how much they were allocated by donors (with or without donor identity, depending on the condition in which an allocation was made), and elicit a second round of reputational evaluations.

Participants are initially asked how much they expect they were given by some of the people for whom they appeared as a recipient in Visit 1 (i.e., how much they expect some of their donors gave them).
A small financial incentive is given for guesses that fall within a range of the actual allocation.
Participants are then informed of all allocations that were made to them.

When the allocation was made in the revealed condition, they are also shown the photograph of the donor, and are asked to judge whether the allocation is not appropriate, appropriate, or very appropriate.
Finally, participants make reputational evaluations for several members of the community, as during Visit 2.
Visit 3 concludes with a debrief stage during which participants are paid the total amount they earned from the games and a second show-up fee.
In (a) Fair (b) Generous the days following the final debriefing visit, members of the research team met informally with community members to discuss their overall experience.
They asked about their perceptions of the experimental protocol and any discomfort it may have caused.
These discussions did not reveal anything concerning.

Since implementing the research protocol, we have returned to TE (India) and AZ (India) sites in January 2026 for a feedback visit, in which we presented early findings to participants and, once more, sought to elicit expressions of any discomfort or unpleasantness that might have emerged after we left the field.
No such discomfort was reported.
Donor-recipient pairings for the various elements were determined through custom R functions meant to ensure an full coverage as possible.

Once the set of participants was determined (i.e., after Visit 1), pairings for all elements were made; adjustments to this (e.g., based on players not completing subsequent visits) were done at the relevant moments.

For the Dictator Game allocation, every participant makes decisions in both conditions and they largely see different recipients across both conditions (with a very low chance of seeing repeat recipients across condition).

For TE, AZ, TM, UP, within each condition, donors are paired with 14 recipients comprising: • two central individuals (i.e., two individuals randomly selected from the top 15% of the (a) Expected (b) Revealed (c) Anonymous network centrality distribution) • two peripheral individuals (i.e., two individuals randomly selected from the bottom 15% of the network centrality distribution).
• 10 further individuals randomly selected from the entire set

For WL, within each condition, donors are paired with 14 recipients comprising: • two central individuals (i.e., two individuals randomly selected from the top 23% of the network centrality distribution) • two peripheral individuals (i.e., two individuals randomly selected from the bottom 23% of the network centrality distribution) • 10 further individuals randomly selected from the entire set For WH, within each condition, donors are paired with 14 recipients comprising: • one central individuals (i.e., one individual randomly selected from the top 25% of the network centrality distribution) • one peripheral individuals (i.e., one individual randomly selected from the bottom 25% of the network centrality distribution) • 10 further individuals randomly selected from the entire set For NP, within each condition, donors are paired with 14 recipients comprising: • two central individuals (i.e., two individuals randomly selected from the top 19% of the network centrality distribution) • two peripheral individuals (i.e., two individuals randomly selected from the bottom 15% of the network centrality distribution) • 10 further individuals randomly selected from the entire set For TZ, within each condition, donors are paired with 15 recipients comprising: • two central individuals (i.e., two individuals randomly selected from the top 15% of the network centrality distribution) • two peripheral individuals (i.e., two individuals randomly selected from the bottom 15% of the network centrality distribution) • 11 further individuals randomly selected from the entire set
The centrality cutoffs were varied across sites so that those identified as central or peripheral matched who the ethnographers knew to hold standing in each community.
These pairings are not quite random-uniform: we use custom functions to try to arrive at the most balanced possible over-sampling of central and peripheral players.
So, central and peripheral players are effectively distributed as evenly as possible across donors.
At the start of Visit 3, before we report allocation decisions to participants, we first elicit their expectations of what 5 of their revealed donors gave to them.
Also, when allocation decisions are being reported, we record recipients' assessment of the "appropriateness" of what was given to them by each revealed donor.
As the contingent nature of these pairings should suggest, a first pass of all pairings is made prior to Visit 2.

Following the completion of data collection for Visit 2, these pairings are revised to account for pairs becoming unviable (if, for example, a player does not complete Visit 2 or if they opt out of a decision).
Replacement pairings are made accordingly.
Participant compensation consists of three key components: • Participation/show-up fees, paid at the ends of Visit 2 and Visit 3.
• Payment from the Dictator Game allocations -Participants make 28 Dictator Game decisions towards known others in the community and will have had a number of decisions made towards them.
We do not pay them for every decision they make, or for every decision made towards them.

We pay participants for a total of four decisions: two decisions are ones where they were a donor to people in the community (they get paid what they chose to keep for themselves), and two decisions are ones where they received money from others (they get paid the amount that other people gave them).

Choosing to "opt out" of any allocation decision has implications for payout: -Payment process for skipped decisions from the donor's perspective -For the donor, if they choose to skip making an allocation towards a person whose photograph they are shown, the decision stops there and they will not choose how to split the money.
The recipient will not be told anything.
However, if this allocation decision is selected for payout, the donor gets 0.
-Payment process of skipped decisions from the recipient's perspective -For the recipient, it is as if the game with the donor (which the donor chose to 'skip') did not happen.
As a result, this will have no consequence for them, and will not impact their final payout (i.e., skipped decisions are never in the pool of decisions from which we draw payouts).
• Payment for accurate expectations -Participants are asked to guess how much five different donors gave them, with close guesses accruing a small additional award.
For our analyses, we use an aggregate network representing the multifaceted social support relationships between adult community residents.
