text.text: Questions are broadly aligned, as all communities are part of the "ENDOW project," which has standardized data collection procedures.
In TE, AZ, WH, WL, and NP, we aimed to survey all adult residents.
In TM and TZ, respondents were limited to male and female household heads.
In Table S6, we show the proportion of game participants for whom we have their own self-reported social support network ties.
text.formatted: In Table <ref type="table">S6</ref>, we show the proportion of game participants for whom we have their own self-reported social support network ties.

text.text: Our aim is to construct a comparable network across the different communities.
This means that we work with a subset of network prompts that is meant to elicit comparable domains of support across the communities.

This entails: • borrowing a week's wages ("monetary loan"), • borrowing food and other basic household items ("household items") • behavioural assistance to women ("female behavioral") and men ("male behavioural") in the sharing unit • socializing and information sharing to women ("female information") and men ("male information") in the sharing unit • assistance from government or NGO officials ("government") • other site-specific assistance outside the community ("external") [this question was not asked in WH and WL]
Note that this is not the full set of questions asked at each community (outlined in the section below).
For example, we do not include questions asking about who people stated came to them for support, instead limiting our attention to just questions about who people stated they went to for support.
As our attention is on social standing and social proximity within the community, we construct networks of all adult residents from which to subsequently construct our centrality measures.
Note that this attention on adult residents means that we exclude people who were named as providing support by survey respondents if they are not resident or not an adult.
We also define residency at the time at which the games were conducted, rather than the time at which the network data were collected.
It is important to note that centrality measures derived from differently constructed networks arrive at similar results.

Alongside the network of adult residents, we considered networks that included: (1) all partners named (so including many partners external to the community), (2) all residents (so including non-adults), (3) all surveyed individuals, and (4) all donors.
Across communities, the Pearson's correlation coefficient of the unweighted PageRank centrality from any combination of these networks was never below 0.71 and was on average 0.95.
We are therefore confident that whichever decision rule is used to define the subset of nodes included in the network, the main results hold.

If we carry forward the decision to use the network of adult residents, then when we construct the distance between residents i and j we consider only the pathways through other adult residents; if they both named a common friend who resided elsewhere, this would not be considered.
Again, making this change from considering only adult residents to the most expansive case of considering all partners named results in small changes to relatively few pairings.
Across all sites, 13.2% of the allocation pairings differ in their distance with these changes, and the vast majority of these by only a single step.
Those differences are thus generally small.
Networks constructed in this way are shown in Figure S24.

text.text: Different sampling frames were used in the different communities, resulting in differences in our coverage of network data for adult residents and participants (see Table S6).
text.formatted: Different sampling frames were used in the different communities, resulting in differences in our coverage of network data for adult residents and participants (see Table <ref type="table">S6</ref>).

text.text: Most notably, in TM and TZ it was largely male-and female-household heads who were surveyed for the social network prompts.
This means that for some donors and some pairs of donors-recipients we lack network information (see Table 2).
text.formatted: This means that for some donors and some pairs of donors-recipients we lack network information (see Table <ref type="table">2</ref>).

text.text: To deal with this, we simulate network data based on what has been observed using an exponential random graph model (ERGM) (Krause et al., 2020).
text.formatted: To deal with this, we simulate network data based on what has been observed using an exponential random graph model (ERGM) <ref type="bibr" target="#b48">(Krause et al., 2020)</ref>.

text.text: We note that for TM and TZ, data is clearly not missing at random, so some caution is warranted.

In brief, we fit an ERGM to the network of all adult residents (at the time of the running of the games), where we note which connections could not have been reported due to the relevant person having not been surveyed.

The ERGM includes terms for: the age of i (Age (outgoing)); the age of j (Age (incoming)); the absolute difference in the ages of i and j (Age difference); whether i and j are the same gender (Same Gender); the gender of i (Male (outgoing)); the gender of j (Male (incoming)); whether j is a person of high status / a leader in the community (High status (incoming)); whether i and j are of the same social group, which could refer to caste, religion, or tribal group (Same Group); the coefficient of biological relatedness between i and j (with, e.g., a value of 0.5 representing a tie between a parent and child or between full siblings) (Blood Relatedness); the equivalent coefficient for relatedness by marriage (with, e.g., a value of 0.5 representing a tie between spouses) (Affinal Relatedness); the normalized square root of the distance between the houses of i and j (Distance); the effect of j naming i on the prospect of i naming j (Reciprocity); and two related terms for triadic closure (i.e., the effect of having friends in common, specifically, geometrically-weighted edge-wise shared partners (GWESP) and geometrically-weighted dyad-wise shared partners (GWDSP)).
The results of that model are then used to simulate 25 networks, where observed dyads are kept fixed and only unobserved dyads are imputed.
This is done using the ergm package in R and its functionality for dealing with missing data (Hunter et al., 2008; Krivitsky et al., 2023; Handcock et al., 2025).
text.formatted: This is done using the ergm package in R and its functionality for dealing with missing data <ref type="bibr" target="#b43">(Hunter et al., 2008;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b49">Krivitsky et al., 2023;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b36">Handcock et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: The alpha decay parameter for the GWESP and GWDSP terms was determined by finding the combination that resulted in the lowest AIC/BIC values for the network.
We evaluated the MCMC diagnostics and goodness of fit measures to ensure that the resulting ERGM appropriately captured the structure of the observed network.
Figure S25 gives examples of what the resulting networks look like.

As explained above, we use an ERGM to impute missing network values and MICE to impute missing values for demographic variables.
Using these techniques, we generate 25 complete datasets, fit a model to each one, and group posterior draws from all models into a single object (following Zhou and Reiter, 2010).
text.formatted: Using these techniques, we generate 25 complete datasets, fit a model to each one, and group posterior draws from all models into a single object (following <ref type="bibr" target="#b92">Zhou and Reiter, 2010)</ref>.

text.text: A side-effect of this procedure is that usual fit diagnostics lose meaning: R-hat values for the combined model, in particular, no longer adequately indicate how well chains have mixed, as between-chain variation is driven by changes in underlying data (across the imputed datasets).
In addition, for computational efficiency, we only use 500 warmup iterations for each of the 25 models, and only take 100 posterior draws per chain.
This low number of posterior draws can lead to instability in the R-hat values and unreliable ESS figures for each of the 25 models (see Table S18).
text.formatted: This low number of posterior draws can lead to instability in the R-hat values and unreliable ESS figures for each of the 25 models (see Table <ref type="table">S18</ref>).

text.text: These diagnostic figures are misleading; they do not reliably indicate problems in the combined model.

To demonstrate that the model obtained from combining imputations is adequate, we follow a two-step strategy: first, in Figures S26, S27, S28 we show that estimated coefficients obtained using multiple imputations are very similar to those obtained with complete-case analysis.
text.formatted: To demonstrate that the model obtained from combining imputations is adequate, we follow a two-step strategy: first, in Figures <ref type="figure" target="#fig_0">S26</ref>, <ref type="figure" target="#fig_0">S27</ref>, S28 we show that estimated coefficients obtained using multiple imputations are very similar to those obtained with complete-case analysis.

text.text: Thus, our conclusions do not rely on imputations; we would have reported the same findings dropping cases with missing values.

The only difference worth mentioning explicitly is for M3 (giving exactly 0), where using imputation leads to a more precise identification of the effect of revelation, with 0, the no-effect value, outside the posterior 95% credibility interval.
Because this is the experimental treatment, for which no value is imputed, we can be confident that the gain in precision is warranted rather than an artifact of imputation.
Second, we show that fit diagnostics for models based on complete-case analysis are adequate.
These diagnostics are shown in Tables S11, S13, S15.

Out of precaution, we did fit models without these random slopes, shown in tables S12, S14, S16.

These latter models may seem preferable in terms of fit, but as outlined in SI P, removing within-donor slopes could lead to anti-conservative estimates for a parameter against which we test one of our hypotheses.
We therefore choose to retain the parameter despite potentially less-than-perfect chain mixing.

In NP (Nepal) and UP (India), we additionally invited participants to make allocations to unknown members of their community.

The protocol was identical to the regular allocations, with the sole difference that the donor was shown a generic pictogram rather than a photo of the recipient, and told that the allocation would go to a randomly selected member of their community (see Fig S40).
text.formatted: The protocol was identical to the regular allocations, with the sole difference that the donor was shown a generic pictogram rather than a photo of the recipient, and told that the allocation would go to a randomly selected member of their community (see Fig <ref type="figure" target="#fig_18">S40</ref>).

text.text: Each donor made one such allocation in the "anonymous" condition and one in the "revealed" condition.
This was done in-app; the unknown alter was presented half-way through each block of regular allocations.
We do not include allocations to unknown alters in the data used to fit the main models.
Table S19 shows the results of a simple model fit only to allocations to unknown alter.
text.formatted: Table <ref type="table">S19</ref> shows the results of a simple model fit only to allocations to unknown alter.

text.text: The results are consistent with our main findings: donors give more when their identity is revealed, even when the recipient is unknown.

Model predictions suggest that the effect size is slightly larger, but of similar magnitude, to what we find in the regular allocations: participants in NP are predicted to give 2.9% [0.8%, 5.1%] more of the total endowment and participants in UP 4.0% [2.4%, 5.5%].
As with the regular allocations, we do not find a clear effect of donor centrality.

text.text: We find large amounts of unexplained heterogeneity at the donor level, but not at the recipient level.
This is true both for random intercepts and random slopes for the effect of revelation, see Figures S17 and S18.
text.formatted: This is true both for random intercepts and random slopes for the effect of revelation, see Figures <ref type="figure">S17</ref> and <ref type="figure">S18</ref>.

text.text: In other words, over and above centrality and distance effects, there are marked differences in how much individual donors give, and how acutely they respond to the effect of revelation.
However, the same does not hold true for recipients: we do not find large amounts of unexplained heterogeneity at this level.
Knowing who is making an allocation yields much better predictions than knowing to whom an allocation is being made.
This is an important consideration for future research, which may do well to focus on donor characteristics when modelling amounts given in the Dictator Game.
NP is a village in the Himalayan foothills of East Nepal.

Residents engage in subsistence agriculture (staple crops: millet, corn, rice), but extreme levels of out-migration have left the community largely bereft of young people, without whom agricultural activity is receding.
The community comprises a wide diversity of caste and ethnic groups, living in physically distinct parts of the village.
Two Dalit communities are present, one of which is almost entirely landless and therefore particularly disadvantaged.
Residents are mainly Hindu, though a young, Nepali form of syncretic Christianity is rapidly gaining ground.
The district capital, a hilly town of approximately 50,000 inhabitants, is an hour's walk / 20-minute slow drive away on unpaved roads.
Kathmandu is the closest city, some 4 hours' drive away.
Ivan Deschenaux has been conducting fieldwork in the community since 2024, following earlier fieldwork elsewhere in East Nepal (Deschenaux, 2019).

UP is a village in Kanpur district, Uttar Pradesh, India.
Agriculture remains an important part of the local economy, with crops including wheat, maize and pulses.
Residents also engage in agricultural and non-agricultural wage labour, private salaried employment and small-scale businesses.

The village is well connected to a nearby town and the city of Kanpur, allowing residents to seek employment beyond the village, particularly in construction, factories, shops and other non-agricultural activities.
The village comprises a mix of caste and religious communities, with considerable differences in their economic and social positions.
There is only one Dalit (Scheduled Caste) community in the village, which, alongside a religious minority community, is among the most economically disadvantaged.
Both communities have limited access to agricultural land and rely more heavily on casual wage labour.
Other caste groups are relatively better positioned in terms of landownership, business activities and employment opportunities, although economic differences also exist within these groups.
In this village, caste remains central to the organisation of economic life and the social relations through which people interact with one another.
Komal Chauhan has been conducting fieldwork in this village since 2024, following earlier fieldwork elsewhere in Uttar Pradesh (Chauhan, 2022).

All sites In all sites, the comprehension checks covered: • Arithmetic: whether the participant could explain how much the donor and recipient would receive, given the initial endowment and a hypothetical allocation.
• Condition: whether the participant could distinguish the two game conditions, that is, explain the difference between the revealed and anonymous condition.

NP and UP only In addition to the above we also checked: • Condition, enhanced Rather than asking only whether participants could tell the two conditions apart, the participant had to demonstrate that they understood who would, and would not, come to know the identity of the donor in four hypothetical cases • Endowment: whether the participant understood that they had the full endowment available for every allocation, rather than a single endowment to be split across all decisions.
• Overall assessment: the research assistant's subjective judgement of the participant's overall comprehension.
For TE, AZ, TM, TZ, WH, and WL, participants were classified into two levels: • Fail.

The participant did not meet the lenient criterion on one or more dimensions: they gave incorrect answers even after repeated explanation, or the research assistant judged their overall comprehension to be very poor.
• Lenient.
The participant passed every dimension, allowing for correct answers reached after additional explanation.
In NP and UP, we additionally recorded how much re-explaining and reprompting participants required to pass comprehension checks, adding the following categories: • Intermediate.

On every dimension, the participant answered correctly either immediately or after a single repetition, and the research assistant judged their overall comprehension to be at least partial ("understood everything well" or "understood some components").
• Strict.

The participant answered every dimension correctly on the first attempt, with no repetition or additional explanation, and the research assistant judged their overall comprehension to be complete ("understood everything well").
Fig S32 and S33 show that including or dropping individuals who fall into the "fail" category, as described above, has no practical effect on estimated coefficients in the main models.
text.formatted: Fig <ref type="figure" target="#fig_21">S32</ref> and S33 show that including or dropping individuals who fall into the "fail" category, as described above, has no practical effect on estimated coefficients in the main models.

text.text: To assess whether the effect of revelation changes with the more granular levels of comprehension we have in NP and UP, we fit an ordered beta regression model with a three-way interaction between donor comprehension level, condition and site (NP and UP) in the predictors.
Figure S34 shows the relative frequency of each comprehension level.
text.formatted: Figure <ref type="figure">S34</ref> shows the relative frequency of each comprehension level.

text.text: Results are shown in Figure S35, which reveals a clear pattern for UP, where the effect is smaller and not clearly distinct from 0 for participants who fail comprehension tests or only pass the "lenient" level, and vastly stronger for participants who pass the "strict" level.
text.formatted: Results are shown in Figure <ref type="figure">S35</ref>, which reveals a clear pattern for UP, where the effect is smaller and not clearly distinct from 0 for participants who fail comprehension tests or only pass the "lenient" level, and vastly stronger for participants who pass the "strict" level.

text.text: The results for NP are less clear: the effect is larger and more clearly identified as non-0 for participants passing the "strict" and "intermediate" checks than those only passing the "lenenient" one.
However, surprisingly, the effect is strongest for participants who fail comprehension checks outright.

Despite this unexplained pattern in NP, we believe these results provide some justification for using granular comprehension tests rather than simple binary ones, when conducting experimental games in remote settings such as those where this study was conducted.
Our design called on participants to make multiple allocations in rapid succession, across two conditions.
We do not formally test whether participants developed fatigue, anchored to past decisions, or otherwise displayed changing patterns of behaviour over time.
The plots included here are meant to offer only a general overview of the possible effects of time and repeated measurement on allocations.
Figure S36 suggests that there was no overall increase or decrease in generosity over time, except in TZ, where participants appear to have given less, on average, during later decisions.
text.formatted: Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_24">S36</ref> suggests that there was no overall increase or decrease in generosity over time, except in TZ, where participants appear to have given less, on average, during later decisions.

text.text: In addition, S37 suggests that a similar pattern may have occured within each condition block in WL.

Figure S38 shows that in most sites, participants showed decreased variation in their allocations as time went by (e.g., the SD for a participant's first five allocations is higher than for allocations 2 to 6, 3 to 7, etc.).
text.formatted: Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_28">S38</ref> shows that in most sites, participants showed decreased variation in their allocations as time went by (e.g., the SD for a participant's first five allocations is higher than for allocations 2 to 6, 3 to 7, etc.).

text.text: Finally, S39 shows the average autocorrelation, across participants, for different lags.
These patterns would be a cause for concern if the order in which participants saw recipients was correlated with the predictors we test hypotheses against, but this is not the case.
Donors saw participants in a randomised order, such that the possible effects of time do not threaten the findings we report.

text.text: While preventing the term from varying leads to better fit diagnostics, it also leads to anti-conservative estimates.
In the case of M2, the posterior 95% percent credibility interval only contains 0 when the term is allowed to vary.
We opt for this more conservative model in the article.

As a robustness check on the ordered beta regression (ordbetareg: Kubinec, 2023) pipeline in brms (Bürkner, 2018), we use a standard multiplex social relations model (Ross et al., 2025) to analyse the same raw data processed so as to be represented as binomial counts: where K = 10 is the maximum allocatable amount, and respondents' donations are expressed as units between 0 and K. In this case, we model-simultaneously-two networks of directed ties: anonymous flows in one layer, and revealed flows in another.

In this case, we model-simultaneously-two networks of directed ties: anonymous flows in one layer, and revealed flows in another.

text.text: The model structure is similar, but not identical, to the one used in the main text.
The covariates we include are the same as in the main model.
However, we include correlated random effects for donor, recipient, and dyad.
These random effects are slightly different than those used in the main model.
As in the main text, STRAND models estimate layer-specific random effects, but STRAND explicitly estimates the correlations in these random effects within and between layers.

The downside of the STRAND models is that we must fit each site separately (so we have no partial pooling), and there is less flexibility in terms of the outcome distribution (though the binomial outcome distribution is not unreasonable).
Results are plotted in Figure S42.
text.formatted: Results are plotted in Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_32">S42</ref>.

text.text: We recover the same general conclusions as in the main model.
Most notably, there is a negative effect of distance on giving in most sites, and there is a positive effect of revelation in most sites.
As in the main model, the STRAND models fail to recover appreciable interactions between revelation and distance or centrality.
